items.prompt: How do the authors of the circuits framework describe its three claims (features, circuits, universality)?
choices: As proven theorems that hold for every trained neural network of any kind
As speculative claims supported mainly by case studies in a vision model
As definitions with no empirical content that experiments could test
As results already replicated across every major language model to date
items.explain: Olah et al. present the three claims as speculative; the supporting evidence is mainly case studies, such as curve detectors in InceptionV1.

items.prompt: Watanabe calls a model “singular” when…
choices: its loss surface has exactly one global minimum, so every training run ends at exactly the same weights
its parameter-to-distribution map is not one-to-one, or its Fisher information is not always positive definite
it is trained on only a single example, so its likelihood carries no information about most of the parameters
its loss is convex in the parameters, so every critical point it has is also a global minimum of the loss
items.explain: Regular models have one-to-one parameter maps and positive definite Fisher information. Singular models, including neural networks, do not, so the BIC approximation with d/2 fails and a learning coefficient (the RLCT) takes its place.

items.prompt: Chen et al. applied SLT to the superposition toy model with two hidden dimensions. What did they report decides which polygon-shaped feature arrangement the Bayesian posterior prefers as the sample size grows?
choices: The order in which the features happened to be initialized before training
The number of parameters in the model, with the smallest arrangement always winning
The local learning coefficient of each arrangement, traded off against its loss
The largest Hessian eigenvalue at each arrangement, and nothing else at all
items.explain: They find regular k-gons are critical points and argue that their local learning coefficients govern Bayesian phase transitions as n grows, trading loss against complexity; the same critical points shape SGD training.

items.prompt: Which statement about estimating the local learning coefficient (LLC) is accurate?
choices: It needs no data at all: it is a fixed property of the architecture and the trained weights alone
It has been proven exact for any network trained with Adam, whatever sampler, temperature or localization settings are used
It is read directly off the rank of the Hessian at the trained solution, so no sampling is needed
It is estimated by sampling weights near the solution, and settings like temperature and localization change the estimate
items.explain: The estimator samples a tempered posterior localized at the solution, using SGLD. Temperature, localization and sampler settings influence the estimate; it was validated on deep linear networks with known values, up to about 100M parameters.

items.prompt: In the stagewise-development study of a roughly 3M-parameter language transformer, what lines up with the LLC-defined stages LM3 and LM4?
choices: Nothing; the stages had no structural or behavioural correlate
The model memorizing its held-out test set word for word
The start and end of the learning-rate warm-up schedule
Formation of previous-token heads and then induction heads
items.explain: Previous-token heads form in LM3 and induction heads in LM4, the same induction circuit studied by Olsson et al. This is an association in small models, not a proof of causation.

items.prompt: Developmental interpretability applies SLT, a theory of Bayesian posteriors, to checkpoints from SGD training. What status does that step have?
choices: A theorem Watanabe proved for stochastic gradient descent runs
A working assumption whose justification is partly empirical
An identity that holds for any optimizer at any learning rate
A definition, so it cannot turn out to be wrong in practice
items.explain: The stagewise authors draw on SLT's framework, but the link from Bayesian analysis to non-equilibrium SGD training is a stated limitation, not a theorem.

items.prompt: How does the Jacobian lens relate to the logit lens?
choices: The J-lens is a tuned lens: it learns a per-layer map trained to match the model's final outputs
They are unrelated: the J-lens uses a separate classifier trained on labelled concepts
The logit lens is the special case where the averaged Jacobian map is replaced by the identity
The J-lens is the logit lens applied only at the final layer, where the two give the same readout
items.explain: The J-lens reads softmax(W_U · norm(J_ℓ h)), with J_ℓ an averaged Jacobian. Setting J_ℓ to the identity gives the logit lens. The tuned lens instead learns its map to match outputs.

items.prompt: Anthropic split each concept vector into a J-space part (6–7% of its variance) and the rest. When they swapped each part to change which item the model reported, what did they find?
choices: Only the larger remainder, about 93% of the variance, had any measurable effect on the report
The J-space part moved the target into the top 5 on 59% of trials, the rest on only 5%
Both parts worked about equally, so the effect tracked each part's share of the variance
Neither part had any effect; only swapping the whole concept vector changed the report
items.explain: In Claude Sonnet 4.5, the small J-space component drove the report (59%, against 88% for pure J-lens vectors), while the remainder succeeded 5% of the time. Clamping the J-space removed even that residual effect.

items.prompt: An independent study ran the multi-hop “swap the unspoken middle step” test on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma 3 27B-it. What is the best-supported reading of its results?
choices: They proved the J-space is a global workspace, because intermediate swaps beat answer swaps in every condition tested
They confirm Claude's 54–70% swap success: intermediate swaps flipped the top answer in most trials on both open models tested
Swaps nudged probabilities as expected but flipped the top answer only 6–11% of the time, and answer swaps often did better
The J-lens produced no readable words on open models, so the swap experiment could not be run at all
items.explain: Zeisler found the intended direction of effect but low top-1 flip rates (6.3–11.1%), with answer swaps ahead in three of four conditions. The author finds the lens useful for forensics but is “not convinced” it is a global workspace.

items.prompt: What do the authors claim about consciousness?
choices: Only functional parallels to “access”: information available for report and reasoning, not experience
Nothing: the paper avoids the topic and never mentions consciousness or global workspace theory
That the J-space proves Claude feels emotions, because words such as panic appear in its readouts
That Claude is phenomenally conscious, since the J-space shows the same signature as human conscious experience
items.explain: The paper takes no position on subjective experience. The blog states “Our experiments don't show Claude can have experiences, or feel things in the way humans do.”

items.prompt: In the model xₜ₊₁ = A xₜ + B uₜ, yₜ = C xₜ, which matrix alone determines how the state evolves when the input is zero?
choices: A
C
B
None; it depends on C and B together
items.explain: With uₜ = 0 the update is xₜ₊₁ = A xₜ, so the free response is xₜ = Aᵗ x₀. B maps inputs into the state and C maps the state to the outputs.

items.prompt: A discrete-time linear recurrence xₖ = A xₖ₋₁ + B uₖ has diagonal A with eigenvalues λⱼ. Which condition makes the state decay to zero from any starting point when the input is zero?
choices: The trace of A is below 1
Every λⱼ has negative real part
Every λⱼ is real
Every |λⱼ| < 1
items.explain: Powers λⱼᵏ decay only when |λⱼ| < 1; the LRU paper uses this condition to keep its learned recurrence stable. Negative real part is the continuous-time condition, not the discrete-time one.

items.prompt: Kalman's 1960 paper shows that the optimal filtering (Wiener) problem is the dual of which problem?
choices: The noise-free optimal regulator problem
Fourier series convergence
Training a perceptron
The travelling-salesman problem
items.explain: Kalman states that the Wiener filtering problem is the dual of the noise-free optimal regulator problem and that the mathematical background of the two is identical, so a solution method for one carries over to the other.

items.prompt: An ARX model predicts yₜ from past outputs yₜ₋₁, yₜ₋₂, … and past inputs uₜ₋₁, uₜ₋₂, … with unknown coefficients. Why can those coefficients be fitted by ordinary least squares?
choices: The coefficients enter the prediction linearly, so it is a linear regression on a vector of past values
Because the system must be stable
Because ARX models have no inputs
Because the noise is always zero
items.explain: Stacking past outputs and inputs into a regression vector makes the prediction linear in the unknown parameters; Ljung calls ARX plus least squares the archetype of system identification.

items.prompt: Compared with plain least squares, what does the ridge penalty λ‖θ‖² do?
choices: Forces exactly half of the weights to be zero
Removes the need for training data
Pulls the weights toward zero, trading a little fit for lower sensitivity to noise
Makes the model nonlinear
items.explain: Ridge adds λI to XᵀX, shrinking the coefficients; under Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior on the weights it equals the posterior mean. Exact zeros are what the L1 (lasso) penalty tends to produce.

items.prompt: For the loss L(θ) = ½‖Xθ − y‖², gradient descent gives θₖ₊₁ = (I − ηXᵀX) θₖ + ηXᵀy. Viewed as a linear system in θ, when does it converge?
choices: Only when XᵀX is diagonal
When 0 < η < 2 / (largest eigenvalue of XᵀX), so every eigenvalue 1 − ηλ of I − ηXᵀX lies strictly between −1 and 1 (directions with λ = 0, which the data never constrain, simply stay put)
For any η > 0, because the loss is convex
Only when η = 1
items.explain: The iteration matrix I − ηXᵀX has eigenvalues 1 − ηλᵢ, which lie strictly between −1 and 1 for every nonzero λᵢ exactly when 0 < η < 2/λmax; directions with λᵢ = 0 are never driven and stay put. Convexity guarantees a single minimum value but not that a large step converges; too large a learning rate overshoots and diverges.

items.prompt: What does backpropagation compute?
choices: A closed-form global minimum of the loss
The best learning rate
The network's output for a new input
The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, by applying the chain rule backwards through the network
items.explain: Backpropagation multiplies local derivatives from the output back to the inputs to obtain all gradients, at a small constant multiple of the cost of one forward pass; gradient descent then uses those gradients to update the weights.

items.prompt: Why does a two-layer network y = W₂ σ(W₁ x) need the nonlinearity σ?
choices: It keeps the weights positive
It is needed only for image inputs
It makes training faster but changes nothing else
Without it, W₂W₁ is a single matrix, so the network is just one linear map
items.explain: Two stacked linear maps collapse into one linear map; the elementwise nonlinearity (such as ReLU) is what lets depth represent nonlinear functions.

items.prompt: An RNN layer computes xₖ = σ(A xₖ₋₁ + B uₖ), yₖ = C xₖ + D uₖ. If σ is replaced by the identity function, what is the layer?
choices: A discrete-time linear state-space model with learned A, B, C, D
An attention layer
A Kalman filter
A feed-forward network with no memory
items.explain: With σ the identity, the update is exactly xₖ = A xₖ₋₁ + B uₖ, yₖ = C xₖ + D uₖ. It still has memory through the state, but it is not a Kalman filter, which needs a noise model and a computed gain.

items.prompt: S4 can compute its output as a convolution with the kernel (CB̄, CĀB̄, CĀ²B̄, …). In control terms, what is this kernel?
choices: The controllability Gramian
The impulse response (Markov parameters) of the discretized system
The transfer function's poles
The Kalman gain sequence
items.explain: For a linear time-invariant system starting from rest, the output is the input convolved with the impulse response C Āᵏ B̄; S4 uses this to train in parallel and the recurrence to generate step by step.
